drills.q: Recite the 8 phases of a 45-minute design round with their minute budgets.
drills.a: 0-2 restate + scope contract; 2-7 requirements (3-5 FRs capped, NFR table, out-of-scope declared); 7-12 numbers you will actually use; 12-17 API signatures; 17-24 data model + partition keys; 24-32 architecture; 32-38 scale; 38-43 failure modes; 43-45 wrap. Architecture must be on the board by minute 32.

drills.q: Convert 'it should be fast' into a designable requirement, then check it against physics.
drills.a: Fast for which endpoint, at which percentile, under what load: p99 of GET /feed under 200 ms at 15k peak QPS measured server-side at the gateway. Physics check: 200 ms accommodates one intra-region round trip (~0.5 ms) plus a cache hit, but not three sequential cross-region calls at 75-230 ms each. If the requirement and topology conflict, that is a design-invalidating finding, not a tuning problem.

drills.q: Give three high-value clarifying questions for 'design Twitter' and say what each decides.
drills.a: Read:write ratio (100:1 justifies precomputing timelines; 2:1 makes read-time merge cheaper). Fanout distribution / do we have 50M-follower accounts (decides fanout-on-write vs hybrid). Chronological or ranked (ranked destroys precomputation because the ordering depends on the reader). Each names two alternatives leading to different designs.

drills.q: Write the feed read and post write endpoints, and name the five points each design detail banks.
drills.a: POST /v1/posts with Authorization + Idempotency-Key, body {text, client_ts}, 201 {post_id, created_at}, errors 400/401/409/429. GET /v1/feed?limit=20&cursor=<opaque> returning items + next_cursor. Points: /v1/ versioning; idempotency key with stored key-to-response and TTL beyond the retry window; cursor not offset because offset skips and duplicates rows on an insert-heavy list; 429 in the contract means a rate limiter belongs in the diagram; 202 elsewhere encodes async fanout before any queue is drawn.

drills.q: For a Twitter-style feed, name every table, its partition key, and whether its main query is single-partition.
drills.a: users(user_id) point read. posts(post_id hash) point read; author-scoped listing is a separate access pattern to defer. follows partitioned by follower_id serves 'who do I follow' single-partition, but fanout needs 'who follows X', which is the reverse, so an inverted table or secondary index on followee_id is required. timeline((user_id, created_at DESC, post_id)) partitioned by user_id, so the feed read is a single-partition ordered range scan of ~20 narrow (~40 B) rows.

drills.q: You are asked to design a notification service for 10M users across email/SMS/push. What is the number that reshapes the whole design, and how do you get it?
drills.a: Cost. 10M users x 5 notifications/day = 5x10^7/day; if 10% go over SMS at ~$0.007/message that is 5x10^6 x $0.007 = $35k/day, about $1M/month. So the expensive failure is a double-send, not downtime, which makes the dedup store the most important component in the diagram and makes Idempotency-Key a required header rather than optional.

drills.q: You drew a cache. Pre-empt the five questions an interviewer will ask about it.
drills.a: Key (timeline:{user_id}); value and size (sorted set capped at 800 entries x ~40 B payload, but budget ~100 B/member because a zset past 128 members becomes a skiplist); TTL and eviction (7-day TTL for inactive users, allkeys-lru under a memory cap); invalidation (write-through on fanout, delete on unfollow); and the assumed hit rate (95%, and the design must survive 0% on cold restart via single-flight coalescing and a jittered warm-up).

drills.q: Your design has six components. Rank the bottlenecks at 10x traffic and justify the ordering.
drills.a: Memory-bound state first (Redis timelines at 50M x 800 x 40 B is ~1.6 TB payload and scales with users, not traffic), single-writer state second (Postgres at 500 to 5,000 write QPS is survivable on one primary with faster storage), stateless tiers last because they only cost more. Then fix Redis without adding hardware: cut the cap 800 to 200 (4x), stop precomputing for the 60-70% inactive users, and pack the member to 8 bytes.

drills.q: Mid-answer, the interviewer says the top account has 200M followers, not the 500 average you assumed. Recover.
drills.a: Name the statistical error: the mean is wrong for a power-law distribution, so 250k inserts/s is right for the body and meaningless for the tail. One post is 200M inserts, ~8 GB of writes, and >13 minutes of fanout that head-of-line blocks the partition. This changes exactly one decision: hybrid fanout, write-fanout below a threshold (~10k) and read-merge above it. It does not change the API, schema, or read path. And the real key is followers x post_rate, not followers alone.

drills.q: Design a recommendation feed with an LLM-generated summary. Give the cost math and then cut it 100x.
drills.a: 10M DAU x 1 summary/day at 2,000 input + 200 output tokens on a Sonnet-class model ($2/$10 per M) = 10M x (2000x$2 + 200x$10)/10^6 = 10M x $0.006 = $60k/day. Unaffordable, so: generate only on first open (removes the 40-70% who never scroll), cache per (user, feed-version) with an hour TTL so re-opens are free, route non-premium users to a Flash-class model at ~20x lower unit price, and truncate context from 2k to 500 tokens by summarising titles only. Those compose to roughly 100x. The LLM is a budgeted resource with a per-user cap enforced in code, and the summary is async with a deterministic extractive fallback.

drills.q: Give the monthly cost of a 50M-DAU feed system, name the dominant line items, and say which estimate you trust least.
drills.a: Redis 1.6 TB ~ $20-25k; Cassandra cold timelines ~100 TB at 3x replication ~ $10-15k; stateless compute for 15k QPS at ~2k rps/node is 15-20 nodes, low thousands; egress 15k QPS x 6 KB = 90 MB/s = ~230 TB/month at $0.05-0.09/GB = $12-20k. Total order $60-80k/month, dominated by Redis and egress. Least confident: egress, because it depends on payload size and CDN offload ratio, both guessed, and it is the line most likely wrong by 3x.

drills.q: When should you deliberately abandon this procedure, and what invariant survives?
drills.a: When the interviewer names the area they want (follow them, compress the rest to stated assumptions); when the round has no scale dimension (front-end design, developer experience, migration strategy) so capacity arithmetic is noise; when you are handed an existing architecture to critique, which is the scale and failure phases only; and when the prompt is ML-shaped, where numbers become token/latency/cost budgets and the data model becomes feature store and index design. The surviving invariant: no box before a requirement or number that produced it.
